notes.text: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel's Network File System Daemon (NFSD). A use-after-free vulnerability can occur during the blocked-lock reaping process. This happens when a client's lock owner, without a proper reference to keep the client alive, leads to the client being prematurely freed. This can result in memory corruption when the system attempts to access freed memory, potentially leading to a denial of service or arbitrary code execution.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: kernel: NFSD: Prevent client use-after-free during blocked-lock reaping
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: A use-after-free flaw rated IMPORTANT by Red Hat was found in the Linux kernel's NFS server (NFSD) blocked-lock handling. When the per-network-namespace laundromat reaps a blocked lock whose lock owner holds only a raw pointer to its nfs4_client, without any reference keeping that client alive, a concurrent client expiry can free the client before nfs4_put_stateowner() runs, causing the client's cl_lock to be dereferenced in freed memory. This memory corruption can lead to a kernel panic (denial of service) or potentially arbitrary code execution. Exploitation requires winning a race condition between blocked-lock reaping and forced client expiry on the NFS server, which makes reliable exploitation difficult. Red Hat products that ship the affected kernel code are impacted, including Red Hat Enterprise Linux (kernel and kernel-rt) and Red Hat In-Vehicle OS (kernel); a fix is being pursued by the responsible engineering teams. The kernel-ivos-qualcomm components in Red Hat In-Vehicle OS are not affected because the vulnerable code is not present. Red Hat rates this flaw lower (CVSS 7.0, IMPORTANT) than the upstream CVE.org assessment (CVSS 9.8, CRITICAL) because triggering the flaw requires a successful race on the server rather than a straightforward unauthenticated network attack.

notes.text: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel's SUNRPC (Sun Remote Procedure Call) component. Improper handling of credential data during the decoding process can lead to a dangling pointer, a form of memory corruption. This issue may allow a remote attacker to cause a denial of service by triggering early decode failures, leading to incorrect state management and potentially system instability.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: kernel: SUNRPC: Zero rpc_gss_wire_cred at svcauth_gss_decode_credbody() entry
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: A flaw of moderate impact was found in the Linux kernel's SUNRPC subsystem, in the server-side GSS credential decoding path svcauth_gss_decode_credbody(). The function writes the caller's rpc_gss_wire_cred field by field and assigns gc_ctx.len only on the success tail, while the destination storage (svcdata->clcred in the per-svc_rqst gss_svc_data) is pooled and reused across requests. Early decode failures therefore leave partially decoded state mixed with residue from the previous request. In the sharpest case, the trailing body_len tightness check leaves gc_ctx.data pointing into the current request's XDR pages while gc_ctx.len retains a stale value from a prior request; once those pages are released, the pooled credential carries a dangling pointer paired with a stale length, which length-driven consumers such as gss_svc_searchbyctx() may otherwise walk, a form of memory corruption. Per the CVE description, a remote attacker able to trigger early decode failures against an RPC service using GSS authentication (for example NFS with RPCSEC_GSS) could use this issue to cause a denial of service through incorrect state management and system instability. Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9 and 10, Red Hat In-Vehicle OS 2, and OpenShift Container Platform releases built on RHEL 9 CoreOS are affected, and fixes are being pursued for those streams. RHEL 6, 7, 8, and 9.2, and OpenShift Container Platform releases built on RHEL 8 CoreOS, are not affected because the vulnerable code is not present in those kernels. Red Hat's severity assessment (impact Moderate, CVSS 3.1 score 7.0, vector AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) differs significantly from the upstream CVEORG rating of 9.8 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H): the Red Hat vector reflects a local attack vector with high attack complexity and some privileges required, whereas the upstream record treats the flaw as remotely exploitable without privileges; the primary documented consequence is denial of service.

A remote peer can exploit this issue by transmitting a malformed Write or Reply chunk with a segment count of zero. Because the kernel fails to validate that the segment count is greater than zero, it accepts and links degenerate chunk structures onto internal processing lists. This flaw may result in unexpected memory traversal or a Denial of Service (DoS).

notes.text:
A flaw of moderate impact was found in the Linux kernel's Remote Procedure Call over Remote Direct Memory Access (RPC-over-RDMA) server component (svcrdma) as shipped in Red Hat Enterprise Linux and Red Hat In-Vehicle OS. The XDR chunk validation (xdr_check_write_chunk()) only rejected segment counts above the allowed maximum, so a Write or Reply chunk with a segment count of zero passed the range check, and a degenerate zero-segment chunk structure was linked onto the server's internal parsed chunk lists. A remote peer able to send requests to the svcrdma transport could transmit such a malformed chunk, which could lead to unexpected memory traversal or a denial of service of the affected kernel. Confidentiality and integrity are not affected; the impact is limited to availability.

Red Hat Enterprise Linux 6 is out of support scope, and Red Hat Enterprise Linux 7 (kernel and kernel-rt) as well as the Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8.4 z-stream are not affected because the vulnerable code is not present in those kernels. The affected Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8, 9, and 10 update streams (including kernel-rt) and Red Hat In-Vehicle OS 2 are affected, and fixes are being pursued through the delegated update streams.

The CVE.org record scores this flaw 9.1 (Critical) using a network attack vector with high confidentiality and availability impact, whereas Red Hat scores it 5.5 (Moderate) with no confidentiality or integrity impact, reflecting Red Hat's assessment of the limited security impact on the affected kernel.

Restrict unprivileged access to the perf event subsystem by setting the `kernel.perf_event_paranoid` sysctl parameter.

1. Apply the setting immediately:

sysctl -w kernel.perf_event_paranoid=3

Restrict network access to the `rpcbind` service on port 111 to trusted systems. This can be achieved by configuring firewall rules to limit inbound connections. For example, using `firewalld` on Red Hat Enterprise Linux:

```bash
# To allow access only from a specific trusted network (e.g., 192.168.1.0/24)
firewall-cmd --permanent --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="192.168.1.0/24" port port="111" protocol="tcp" accept'
firewall-cmd --permanent --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="192.168.1.0/24" port port="111" protocol="udp" accept'
firewall-cmd --reload
```

If `rpcbind` is only required for local services, ensure it is configured to listen only on the loopback interface or is otherwise protected from external network exposure. Applying these firewall rules will take effect immediately upon `firewall-cmd --reload` and may temporarily interrupt existing connections to `rpcbind`.

notes.text: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel. A local attacker or untrusted guest virtual machine can exploit this vulnerability by transmitting network packets containing malformed checksum metadata into the IPv4 networking subsystem. notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This IMPORTANT-severity flaw affects the Linux kernel as shipped in Red Hat products, including the kernel and kernel-rt packages in Red Hat Enterprise Linux and the kernels shipped in Red Hat In-Vehicle OS. The IPv4 networking subsystem does not validate packet checksum metadata before completing a checksum: when a packet with a malformed checksum_start value enters the IPv4 stack, skb_checksum_help() can write out of bounds and corrupt the network header and other kernel memory (CWE-787). A local attacker or an untrusted guest virtual machine able to transmit such packets into an affected host could exploit this to crash the system (denial of service), disclose sensitive kernel memory, or potentially execute arbitrary code on the host. Red Hat tracks this flaw as a KEV active-exploit case. All currently tracked Red Hat product streams are marked affected, and fixes are being pursued by the responsible Red Hat product teams under delegated resolution. Red Hat's severity differs from the upstream assessment: Red Hat assigns a CVSS 3.1 score of 8.8 (IMPORTANT, AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H), while the CVE.org record assigns 9.3 (CRITICAL, AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H); the two assessments differ on the privileges-required metric.

cwe.name: Improper Handling of Highly Compressed Data (Data Amplification)

notes.text: A flaw was found in Tornado. A remote malicious server can cause a Denial of Service (DoS) when an application using the CurlAsyncHTTPClient component fetches an untrusted web address. Because the client fails to enforce limits on incoming response sizes, the attacker can return a small, highly compressed payload (a decompression bomb) that expands to an enormous size. This unbounded memory consumption exhausts system resources and crashes the application.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: tornado: Tornado: Denial of Service via decompression bomb in CurlAsyncHTTPClient
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability has been rated as Important because an untrusted remote server can remotely terminate an application process through memory exhaustion without requiring credentials. By default, Tornado deploys the SimpleAsyncHTTPClient implementation, which includes built-in thresholds for decompressed and raw payload sizes and remains unaffected by this flaw. However, systems that explicitly configure CurlAsyncHTTPClient—typically enabled for custom proxy routing or advanced transport options—bypass these protections and do not enforce body size constraints. When such client applications fetch resources from compromised or malicious web endpoints, the resulting decompression bomb can consume all available system memory, leading to an immediate denial of service.

Restrict outbound HTTP client requests to trusted destinations and avoid using the CurlAsyncHTTPClient backend when fetching untrusted web content.

1. Application configuration: Configure Tornado applications to utilize the default SimpleAsyncHTTPClient instead of CurlAsyncHTTPClient, provided specialized libcurl functionality (such as custom proxy configurations or specific TLS options) is not required. The default client enforces strict size boundaries on compressed and uncompressed response bodies.
2. Network egress filtering: Implement firewall rules or egress network policies to restrict outbound HTTP/HTTPS connections exclusively to verified, trustworthy endpoints, preventing the client from contacting potentially malicious third-party servers.
3. Operational controls: Ensure that user-supplied or untrusted URLs are validated, sanitized, or rejected before initiating outbound retrieval requests.

Caveats: Switching the HTTP client backend from CurlAsyncHTTPClient to SimpleAsyncHTTPClient may disrupt services that depend on libcurl-specific features. Enforcing egress filtering may block connections to unlisted external services.

notes.text:
The system certificate authority (CA) store in Red Hat products, distributed via ca-certificates RPM packages, included multiple root CA certificates of authorities, which signed intermediate CA certificates with weak private keys issued by the eMudhra certificate authority. A man-in-the-middle attacker could use this flaw to issue certificates for arbitrary host names signed by the weak intermediate CA certificates, which would be considered trusted by a TLS/SSL client using system CA store and cause such clients to connect to malicious sites.

Due to inability to only distrust specific intermediate certificates in all clients using the system CA store, root CA certificates of authorities that signed weak intermediate CA certificates are being removed.

notes.text:
The kernel packages contain the Linux kernel, the core of any Linux operating system.

Security Fix(es):

* kernel: tcp: restrict SO_ATTACH_FILTER to priv users (CVE-2026-53236)

* kernel: fuse: re-lock request before replacing page cache folio (CVE-2026-53388)

* kernel: writeback: fix race between cgroup_writeback_umount() and inode_switch_wbs() (CVE-2026-64378)

* kernel: net: gro: fix double aggregation of flush-marked skbs (CVE-2026-68136)

* kernel: net/packet: avoid fanout hook re-registration after unregister (CVE-2026-68338)

* kernel: net/iucv: fix use-after-free of a severed iucv_path (CVE-2026-68140)

* kernel: net/sched: serialize qdisc_rtab_list against concurrent get/put (CVE-2026-68138)

* kernel: ipvs: reload ip header after head reallocation (CVE-2026-68476)

* kernel: mptcp: options: reset DSS fields in case of unexpected size (CVE-2026-80586)

* kernel: usb: usbfs: fix use-after-free of usb_device in usbdev_release() (CVE-2026-80824)

* kernel: smb: client: clear setuid/setgid bit on write with cifsacl/modefromsid/posix extensions (CVE-2026-89638)

* kernel: net/iucv: filter frames in afiucv_hs_rcv() by ingress device (CVE-2026-81003)

* kernel: ipv4: validate checksum_start before completing checksum
(CVE-2026-99999)

Bug Fix(es) and Enhancement(s):

* Backport 6785011f8b16 ("ipv4: validate checksum_start before completing checksum") [rhel-8.10.z] (JIRA:RHEL-280584)

For more details about the security issue(s), including the impact, a CVSS score, acknowledgments, and other related information, refer to the CVE page(s) listed in the References section.

notes.text: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel. This use-after-free vulnerability exists in the `net/iucv` component. When a peer severs a connection, message notifications that still reference the freed connection path remain in a queue. A subsequent attempt to process these stale notifications can lead to memory corruption, potentially resulting in a system crash (denial of service) or allowing an attacker to execute arbitrary code.

notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: A use-after-free flaw was found in the Linux kernel's net/iucv (AF_IUCV socket) implementation, rated IMPORTANT by Red Hat Product Security. The af_iucv implementation queues not-yet-received message notifications on a per-socket message queue, with each notification holding a raw pointer to the connection's iucv_path. When a peer severs the connection, iucv_sever_path() frees that path but leaves the queued notifications in place; a later recvmsg() drains the queue via iucv_process_message_q() and hands the stale pointer to message_receive(), resulting in a use-after-free of the freed iucv_path. A local attacker able to open and use AF_IUCV sockets could race a peer severing the connection against processing of the queued messages, causing kernel memory corruption that can result in a system crash (denial of service) or, potentially, execution of arbitrary code. Red Hat Enterprise Linux 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10 (kernel and kernel-rt) and Red Hat In-Vehicle OS are affected; fixes are being pursued through the respective kernel teams for the affected product streams. Red Hat Product Security scored this flaw CVSS 3.1 7.0 (AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H), lower than the upstream CVEORG score of 8.8 (AV:A/AC:L/PR:N), because successful exploitation requires local access with the ability to create AF_IUCV socket connections and depends on high attack complexity due to the timing-sensitive race between connection severing and message queue processing.

The vulnerability affects the Multipath TCP (MPTCP) feature in the Linux kernel. To mitigate this issue, MPTCP can be disabled by preventing the `mptcp` kernel module from loading. To disable the `mptcp` module: 1. Create a new file `/etc/modprobe.d/disable-mptcp.conf` with the following content: `install mptcp /bin/true
blacklist mptcp` 2. Regenerate the initramfs to ensure the change takes effect on boot: `sudo dracut -f -v` 3. Reboot the system for the changes to take effect. Disabling MPTCP may impact network performance or functionality for applications that rely on Multipath TCP.

notes.text: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel's USB subsystem (usbfs). An unprivileged local attacker with read/write access to a /dev/bus/usb node could exploit a use-after-free vulnerability. This occurs because the usb_device structure is prematurely freed before all pending operations are completed. Successful exploitation of this memory corruption flaw could lead to a system crash or potentially privilege escalation.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: kernel: usb: usbfs: fix use-after-free of usb_device in usbdev_release()
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: An Important severity use-after-free flaw was found in the Linux kernel usbfs (USB user-space) subsystem, affecting the kernel and kernel-rt packages in Red Hat Enterprise Linux and other Red Hat products that ship the Red Hat kernel. In usbdev_release(), the reference to the struct usb_device is dropped before the list of completed asynchronous URBs is drained, and the drain path (free_async() calling dec_usb_memory_use_count()) then reads back through the already-freed device, for example via bus_to_hcd(ps->dev->bus). An unprivileged local attacker with read/write access to a /dev/bus/usb device node could mmap() the file descriptor, submit an asynchronous URB whose buffer lies inside that mapping, wait for the device to be unplugged so that the usbfs reference becomes the last reference and the device is freed, and then unmap and close the file descriptor, deterministically triggering the use-after-free. Successful exploitation of this memory corruption flaw could lead to a kernel crash (denial of service) or potentially privilege escalation. Red Hat rates this flaw with a CVSS 3.1 score of 7.0 (AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H): although triggering the use-after-free itself is deterministic and not a race, reliably converting it into privilege escalation requires high attack complexity. A fix is being pursued for the affected Red Hat products.

notes.text: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel's AF_IUCV (Advanced Program-to-Program Communication over IUCV) network protocol implementation. The `afiucv_hs_rcv()` function, responsible for receiving frames, does not properly filter incoming frames based on the ingress network device. This oversight allows a local attacker with specific network capabilities or a host on the same HiperSockets segment to send specially crafted frames. Successful exploitation can lead to a Denial of Service (DoS) by exhausting the accept-queue, injecting data into existing sockets, and disrupting established connections.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: kernel: net/iucv: filter frames in afiucv_hs_rcv() by ingress device
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: A flaw rated IMPORTANT by Red Hat Product Security was found in the Linux kernel's AF_IUCV protocol implementation, used for the z/VM IUCV and HiperSockets transports on the s390x (IBM Z) architecture. The afiucv_hs_rcv() receive path selected a target socket from the global socket list by matching only the four 8-byte name fields in the frame's transport header, without checking the network device the frame arrived on. As a result, a frame received on any network device could be delivered to an AF_IUCV socket bound to a different device or to the classic z/VM IUCV transport. A local attacker holding only the CAP_NET_RAW capability inside an unprivileged user and network namespace could send a raw ETH_P_AF_IUCV frame on its own loopback device and have it matched against sockets in the initial network namespace; similarly, a host on the same shared HiperSockets segment could direct frames at sockets bound to a different HiperSockets device. Successful exploitation could exhaust a listening socket's accept queue (denial of service), inject data into existing AF_IUCV connections, control the peer identity of accepted child sockets, and disrupt or kill established connections. Multiple Red Hat Enterprise Linux kernel and kernel-rt update streams and Red Hat In-Vehicle OS kernel streams are affected, and fixes are being pursued in the respective product streams; the kernel-ivos-qualcomm component of Red Hat In-Vehicle OS is not affected because the vulnerable code is not present in that kernel. The Red Hat severity of IMPORTANT (CVSS 3.1 score 7.0, AV:L/AC:H/PR:L) is lower than the upstream CVE.org rating of 8.1 (AV:A/AC:L/PR:N): Red Hat assessed the dominant exploitation path as local, requiring privileges and high attack complexity, whereas the upstream rating emphasizes the adjacent-network HiperSockets vector requiring no privileges. Note that AF_IUCV over HiperSockets provides no per-connection authentication, so the fix reduces the attack surface to peers present on the same HiperSockets segment but does not change that protocol-level property.

notes.text: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel's Server Message Block (SMB) client. When a file with the setuid or setgid bit is written to on certain Common Internet File System (CIFS) mounts (specifically those using 'cifsacl', 'modefromsid' options, or SMB3.1.1 POSIX extensions), the kernel fails to properly clear these bits on the server. Mount SMB/CIFS shares with the `nosuid` mount option to prevent setuid and setgid binaries from executing with elevated permissions, or prevent the `cifs` module from loading if network SMB shares are not needed.

1. Apply `nosuid` to an active mount point:
```
mount -o remount,nosuid /path/to/cifs/mount
```

2. Persist this setting by ensuring `nosuid` is present in the mount options within `/etc/fstab`:
```
//server/share /mnt/cifs cifs credentials=/etc/samba/creds,nosuid 0 0
```

3. Alternatively, if CIFS mounts are not required on the system, disable autoloading of the kernel module:
```
echo "install cifs /bin/true" > /etc/modprobe.d/cifs.conf
```

Caveats:
Enforcing `nosuid` prevents any executable located on the mount point from running with elevated setuid or setgid privileges. Blacklisting the `cifs` module prevents all SMB/CIFS network file systems from mounting. Remounting filesystems can disrupt ongoing read and write operations.

notes.text: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel. A local attacker or untrusted guest virtual machine can exploit this vulnerability by transmitting network packets containing malformed checksum metadata into the IPv4 networking subsystem. This failure to validate checksum metadata can corrupt memory during packet handling, potentially leading to arbitrary code execution on the host, a system crash resulting in Denial of Service (DoS), or information disclosure of sensitive memory.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: kernel: ipv4: validate checksum_start before completing checksum
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This IMPORTANT-severity flaw affects the Linux kernel as shipped in Red Hat products, including the kernel and kernel-rt packages in Red Hat Enterprise Linux and the kernels shipped in Red Hat In-Vehicle OS. The IPv4 networking subsystem does not validate packet checksum metadata before completing a checksum: when a packet with a malformed checksum_start value enters the IPv4 stack, skb_checksum_help() can write out of bounds and corrupt the network header and other kernel memory (CWE-787). A local attacker or an untrusted guest virtual machine able to transmit such packets into an affected host could exploit this to crash the system (denial of service), disclose sensitive kernel memory, or potentially execute arbitrary code on the host. Red Hat tracks this flaw as a KEV active-exploit case. All currently tracked Red Hat product streams are marked affected, and fixes are being pursued by the responsible Red Hat product teams under delegated resolution. Red Hat's severity differs from the upstream assessment: Red Hat assigns a CVSS 3.1 score of 8.8 (IMPORTANT, AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H), while the CVE.org record assigns 9.3 (CRITICAL, AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H); the two assessments differ on the privileges-required metric.

notes.text:
The kernel-rt packages provide the Real Time Linux Kernel, which enables fine-tuning for systems with extremely high determinism requirements.

* kernel: fuse: re-lock request before replacing page cache folio (CVE-2026-53388)

* kernel: net/sched: serialize qdisc_rtab_list against concurrent get/put (CVE-2026-68138)

* kernel: ipvs: reload ip header after head reallocation (CVE-2026-68476)

* kernel: selinux: avoid sk_socket dereference in selinux_sctp_bind_connect() (CVE-2026-72242)

* kernel: mptcp: options: reset DSS fields in case of unexpected size (CVE-2026-80586)

* kernel: usb: usbfs: fix use-after-free of usb_device in usbdev_release() (CVE-2026-80824)

* kernel: smb: client: clear setuid/setgid bit on write with cifsacl/modefromsid/posix extensions (CVE-2026-89638)

* kernel: net/iucv: filter frames in afiucv_hs_rcv() by ingress device (CVE-2026-81003)

This information disclosure could potentially be used to aid further attacks.

notes.text: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel's Filesystem in Userspace (FUSE) component. The `fuse_try_move_folio()` function, responsible for managing page cache folios, fails to re-lock a request after initially unlocking it on a successful path. This oversight allows another function, `fuse_chan_abort()`, to prematurely free critical input/output arguments (`fuse_io_args`). Consequently, subsequent operations attempting to access these freed arguments can lead to a use-after-free vulnerability, potentially allowing an attacker to cause a system crash or execute arbitrary code.

notes.text: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel's Generic Receive Offload (GRO) networking subsystem. An attacker could exploit this by sending specially crafted network packets that cause a double aggregation of flush-marked socket buffers (skbs). This issue arises from a missing flush check, which allows already-processed packets to be re-aggregated, corrupting the internal data structure. This corruption leads to an invalid state when the system attempts to process these packets, triggering a kernel panic and resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS).

notes.text: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel. This use-after-free vulnerability exists in the `net/iucv` component. When a peer severs a connection, message notifications that still reference the freed connection path remain in a queue. A subsequent attempt to process these stale notifications can lead to memory corruption, potentially resulting in a system crash (denial of service) or allowing an attacker to execute arbitrary code.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: kernel: net/iucv: fix use-after-free of a severed iucv_path
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: A use-after-free flaw was found in the Linux kernel's net/iucv (AF_IUCV socket) implementation, rated IMPORTANT by Red Hat Product Security. The af_iucv implementation queues not-yet-received message notifications on a per-socket message queue, with each notification holding a raw pointer to the connection's iucv_path. When a peer severs the connection, iucv_sever_path() frees that path but leaves the queued notifications in place; a later recvmsg() drains the queue via iucv_process_message_q() and hands the stale pointer to message_receive(), resulting in a use-after-free of the freed iucv_path. A local attacker able to open and use AF_IUCV sockets could race a peer severing the connection against processing of the queued messages, causing kernel memory corruption that can result in a system crash (denial of service) or, potentially, execution of arbitrary code. Red Hat Enterprise Linux 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10 (kernel and kernel-rt) and Red Hat In-Vehicle OS are affected; fixes are being pursued through the respective kernel teams for the affected product streams. Red Hat Product Security scored this flaw CVSS 3.1 7.0 (AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H), lower than the upstream CVEORG score of 8.8 (AV:A/AC:L/PR:N), because successful exploitation requires local access with the ability to create AF_IUCV socket connections and depends on high attack complexity due to the timing-sensitive race between connection severing and message queue processing.

The vulnerability affects the Multipath TCP (MPTCP) feature in the Linux kernel. To mitigate this issue, MPTCP can be disabled by preventing the `mptcp` kernel module from loading. To disable the `mptcp` module: 1. Create a new file `/etc/modprobe.d/disable-mptcp.conf` with the following content: `install mptcp /bin/true
blacklist mptcp` 2. Regenerate the initramfs to ensure the change takes effect on boot: `sudo dracut -f -v` 3. Reboot the system for the changes to take effect. Disabling MPTCP may impact network performance or functionality for applications that rely on Multipath TCP.

notes.text: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel's USB subsystem (usbfs). An unprivileged local attacker with read/write access to a /dev/bus/usb node could exploit a use-after-free vulnerability. This occurs because the usb_device structure is prematurely freed before all pending operations are completed. Successful exploitation of this memory corruption flaw could lead to a system crash or potentially privilege escalation.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: kernel: usb: usbfs: fix use-after-free of usb_device in usbdev_release()
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: An Important severity use-after-free flaw was found in the Linux kernel usbfs (USB user-space) subsystem, affecting the kernel and kernel-rt packages in Red Hat Enterprise Linux and other Red Hat products that ship the Red Hat kernel. In usbdev_release(), the reference to the struct usb_device is dropped before the list of completed asynchronous URBs is drained, and the drain path (free_async() calling dec_usb_memory_use_count()) then reads back through the already-freed device, for example via bus_to_hcd(ps->dev->bus). An unprivileged local attacker with read/write access to a /dev/bus/usb device node could mmap() the file descriptor, submit an asynchronous URB whose buffer lies inside that mapping, wait for the device to be unplugged so that the usbfs reference becomes the last reference and the device is freed, and then unmap and close the file descriptor, deterministically triggering the use-after-free. Successful exploitation of this memory corruption flaw could lead to a kernel crash (denial of service) or potentially privilege escalation. Red Hat rates this flaw with a CVSS 3.1 score of 7.0 (AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H): although triggering the use-after-free itself is deterministic and not a race, reliably converting it into privilege escalation requires high attack complexity. A fix is being pursued for the affected Red Hat products.

notes.text: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel's AF_IUCV (Advanced Program-to-Program Communication over IUCV) network protocol implementation. The `afiucv_hs_rcv()` function, responsible for receiving frames, does not properly filter incoming frames based on the ingress network device. This oversight allows a local attacker with specific network capabilities or a host on the same HiperSockets segment to send specially crafted frames. Successful exploitation can lead to a Denial of Service (DoS) by exhausting the accept-queue, injecting data into existing sockets, and disrupting established connections.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: kernel: net/iucv: filter frames in afiucv_hs_rcv() by ingress device
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: A flaw rated IMPORTANT by Red Hat Product Security was found in the Linux kernel's AF_IUCV protocol implementation, used for the z/VM IUCV and HiperSockets transports on the s390x (IBM Z) architecture. The afiucv_hs_rcv() receive path selected a target socket from the global socket list by matching only the four 8-byte name fields in the frame's transport header, without checking the network device the frame arrived on. As a result, a frame received on any network device could be delivered to an AF_IUCV socket bound to a different device or to the classic z/VM IUCV transport. A local attacker holding only the CAP_NET_RAW capability inside an unprivileged user and network namespace could send a raw ETH_P_AF_IUCV frame on its own loopback device and have it matched against sockets in the initial network namespace; similarly, a host on the same shared HiperSockets segment could direct frames at sockets bound to a different HiperSockets device. Successful exploitation could exhaust a listening socket's accept queue (denial of service), inject data into existing AF_IUCV connections, control the peer identity of accepted child sockets, and disrupt or kill established connections. Multiple Red Hat Enterprise Linux kernel and kernel-rt update streams and Red Hat In-Vehicle OS kernel streams are affected, and fixes are being pursued in the respective product streams; the kernel-ivos-qualcomm component of Red Hat In-Vehicle OS is not affected because the vulnerable code is not present in that kernel. The Red Hat severity of IMPORTANT (CVSS 3.1 score 7.0, AV:L/AC:H/PR:L) is lower than the upstream CVE.org rating of 8.1 (AV:A/AC:L/PR:N): Red Hat assessed the dominant exploitation path as local, requiring privileges and high attack complexity, whereas the upstream rating emphasizes the adjacent-network HiperSockets vector requiring no privileges. Note that AF_IUCV over HiperSockets provides no per-connection authentication, so the fix reduces the attack surface to peers present on the same HiperSockets segment but does not change that protocol-level property.

notes.text: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel's Server Message Block (SMB) client. When a file with the setuid or setgid bit is written to on certain Common Internet File System (CIFS) mounts (specifically those using 'cifsacl', 'modefromsid' options, or SMB3.1.1 POSIX extensions), the kernel fails to properly clear these bits on the server. This oversight allows the setuid/setgid bits to persist, which could enable a local attacker to achieve unexpected privilege escalation upon subsequent execution of the affected file.

Mount SMB/CIFS shares with the `nosuid` mount option to prevent setuid and setgid binaries from executing with elevated permissions, or prevent the `cifs` module from loading if network SMB shares are not needed.

1. Apply `nosuid` to an active mount point:
```
mount -o remount,nosuid /path/to/cifs/mount
```

2. Persist this setting by ensuring `nosuid` is present in the mount options within `/etc/fstab`:
```
//server/share /mnt/cifs cifs credentials=/etc/samba/creds,nosuid 0 0
```

3. Alternatively, if CIFS mounts are not required on the system, disable autoloading of the kernel module:
```
echo "install cifs /bin/true" > /etc/modprobe.d/cifs.conf
```

Caveats:
Enforcing `nosuid` prevents any executable located on the mount point from running with elevated setuid or setgid privileges. Blacklisting the `cifs` module prevents all SMB/CIFS network file systems from mounting. Remounting filesystems can disrupt ongoing read and write operations.

notes.text: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel. A local attacker or untrusted guest virtual machine can exploit this vulnerability by transmitting network packets containing malformed checksum metadata into the IPv4 networking subsystem. This failure to validate checksum metadata can corrupt memory during packet handling, potentially leading to arbitrary code execution on the host, a system crash resulting in Denial of Service (DoS), or information disclosure of sensitive memory.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: kernel: ipv4: validate checksum_start before completing checksum
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This IMPORTANT-severity flaw affects the Linux kernel as shipped in Red Hat products, including the kernel and kernel-rt packages in Red Hat Enterprise Linux and the kernels shipped in Red Hat In-Vehicle OS. A local attacker or an untrusted guest virtual machine able to transmit such packets into an affected host could exploit this to crash the system (denial of service), disclose sensitive kernel memory, or potentially execute arbitrary code on the host. Red Hat tracks this flaw as a KEV active-exploit case. All currently tracked Red Hat product streams are marked affected, and fixes are being pursued by the responsible Red Hat product teams under delegated resolution. notes.text: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel. A local attacker or untrusted guest virtual machine can exploit this vulnerability by transmitting network packets containing malformed checksum metadata into the IPv4 networking subsystem. This failure to validate checksum metadata can corrupt memory during packet handling, potentially leading to arbitrary code execution on the host, a system crash resulting in Denial of Service (DoS), or information disclosure of sensitive memory.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: kernel: ipv4: validate checksum_start before completing checksum
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This IMPORTANT-severity flaw affects the Linux kernel as shipped in Red Hat products, including the kernel and kernel-rt packages in Red Hat Enterprise Linux and the kernels shipped in Red Hat In-Vehicle OS. The IPv4 networking subsystem does not validate packet checksum metadata before completing a checksum: when a packet with a malformed checksum_start value enters the IPv4 stack, skb_checksum_help() can write out of bounds and corrupt the network header and other kernel memory (CWE-787). A local attacker or an untrusted guest virtual machine able to transmit such packets into an affected host could exploit this to crash the system (denial of service), disclose sensitive kernel memory, or potentially execute arbitrary code on the host. Red Hat tracks this flaw as a KEV active-exploit case. All currently tracked Red Hat product streams are marked affected, and fixes are being pursued by the responsible Red Hat product teams under delegated resolution. Red Hat's severity differs from the upstream assessment: Red Hat assigns a CVSS 3.1 score of 8.8 (IMPORTANT, AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H), while the CVE.org record assigns 9.3 (CRITICAL, AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H); the two assessments differ on the privileges-required metric.
notes.title: Statement

notes.text: The CVSS score(s) listed for this vulnerability do not reflect the associated product's status, and are included for informational purposes to better understand the severity of this vulnerability.

remediations.details:
For details on how to apply this update, which includes the changes described in this advisory, refer to:

https://access.redhat.com/articles/11258

The system must be rebooted for this update to take effect.

Red Hat recommends treating all kernel errata as security-relevant. Given the kernel's fundamental role, any bug has a higher chance of impacting system security, even if that impact only becomes clear after a fix is published. Therefore, Red Hat prioritizes delivering fixes that improve our customers' overall security posture.

Because of this proactive approach, a patch may be associated with a CVE assignment at a future date. Retroactive CVE assignments are always documented in the corresponding errata and on Red Hat's CVE pages. We strongly advise against delaying updates, as doing so may leave your system exposed when protections are already available.

Mitigation for this issue is either not available or the currently available options do not meet the Red Hat Product Security criteria comprising ease of use and deployment, applicability to widespread installation base, or stability.

notes.text: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel. A local attacker or untrusted guest virtual machine can exploit this vulnerability by transmitting network packets containing malformed checksum metadata into the IPv4 networking subsystem. This failure to validate checksum metadata can corrupt memory during packet handling, potentially leading to arbitrary code execution on the host, a system crash resulting in Denial of Service (DoS), or information disclosure of sensitive memory.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: kernel: ipv4: validate checksum_start before completing checksum
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This IMPORTANT-severity flaw affects the Linux kernel as shipped in Red Hat products, including the kernel and kernel-rt packages in Red Hat Enterprise Linux and the kernels shipped in Red Hat In-Vehicle OS. The IPv4 networking subsystem does not validate packet checksum metadata before completing a checksum: when a packet with a malformed checksum_start value enters the IPv4 stack, skb_checksum_help() can write out of bounds and corrupt the network header and other kernel memory (CWE-787). A local attacker or an untrusted guest virtual machine able to transmit such packets into an affected host could exploit this to crash the system (denial of service), disclose sensitive kernel memory, or potentially execute arbitrary code on the host. Red Hat tracks this flaw as a KEV active-exploit case. All currently tracked Red Hat product streams are marked affected, and fixes are being pursued by the responsible Red Hat product teams under delegated resolution. Red Hat's severity differs from the upstream assessment: Red Hat assigns a CVSS 3.1 score of 8.8 (IMPORTANT, AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H), while the CVE.org record assigns 9.3 (CRITICAL, AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H); the two assessments differ on the privileges-required metric.

notes.text: The CVSS score(s) listed for this vulnerability do not reflect the associated product's status, and are included for informational purposes to better understand the severity of this vulnerability.

remediations.details:
For details on how to apply this update, which includes the changes described in this advisory, refer to:

https://access.redhat.com/articles/11258

The system must be rebooted for this update to take effect.

Red Hat recommends treating all kernel errata as security-relevant. Given the kernel's fundamental role, any bug has a higher chance of impacting system security, even if that impact only becomes clear after a fix is published. Therefore, Red Hat prioritizes delivering fixes that improve our customers' overall security posture.

Because of this proactive approach, a patch may be associated with a CVE assignment at a future date. Retroactive CVE assignments are always documented in the corresponding errata and on Red Hat's CVE pages. We strongly advise against delaying updates, as doing so may leave your system exposed when protections are already available.

Mitigation for this issue is either not available or the currently available options do not meet the Red Hat Product Security criteria comprising ease of use and deployment, applicability to widespread installation base, or stability.

notes.text: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel. A local attacker or untrusted guest virtual machine can exploit this vulnerability by transmitting network packets containing malformed checksum metadata into the IPv4 networking subsystem. This failure to validate checksum metadata can corrupt memory during packet handling, potentially leading to arbitrary code execution on the host, a system crash resulting in Denial of Service (DoS), or information disclosure of sensitive memory.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: kernel: ipv4: validate checksum_start before completing checksum
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This IMPORTANT-severity flaw affects the Linux kernel as shipped in Red Hat products, including the kernel and kernel-rt packages in Red Hat Enterprise Linux and the kernels shipped in Red Hat In-Vehicle OS. The IPv4 networking subsystem does not validate packet checksum metadata before completing a checksum: when a packet with a malformed checksum_start value enters the IPv4 stack, skb_checksum_help() can write out of bounds and corrupt the network header and other kernel memory (CWE-787). A local attacker or an untrusted guest virtual machine able to transmit such packets into an affected host could exploit this to crash the system (denial of service), disclose sensitive kernel memory, or potentially execute arbitrary code on the host. Red Hat tracks this flaw as a KEV active-exploit case. All currently tracked Red Hat product streams are marked affected, and fixes are being pursued by the responsible Red Hat product teams under delegated resolution. Red Hat's severity differs from the upstream assessment: Red Hat assigns a CVSS 3.1 score of 8.8 (IMPORTANT, AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H), while the CVE.org record assigns 9.3 (CRITICAL, AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H); the two assessments differ on the privileges-required metric.

remediations.details:
For details on how to apply this update, which includes the changes described in this advisory, refer to:

https://access.redhat.com/articles/11258

The system must be rebooted for this update to take effect.

Red Hat recommends treating all kernel errata as security-relevant. Given the kernel's fundamental role, any bug has a higher chance of impacting system security, even if that impact only becomes clear after a fix is published. Therefore, Red Hat prioritizes delivering fixes that improve our customers' overall security posture.

Because of this proactive approach, a patch may be associated with a CVE assignment at a future date. Retroactive CVE assignments are always documented in the corresponding errata and on Red Hat's CVE pages. We strongly advise against delaying updates, as doing so may leave your system exposed when protections are already available.

Mitigation for this issue is either not available or the currently available options do not meet the Red Hat Product Security criteria comprising ease of use and deployment, applicability to widespread installation base, or stability.
